note: Refreshed every week by the program's research task. Each item says what changed, why it matters to a data engineer or architect, and how to test the claim yourself.

items.title: Snowflake: read and write another account's Iceberg tables through Horizon Catalog, with no secrets to manage (GA)
items.summary: Announced on 1 November 2026. A Snowflake account can now read and write Apache Iceberg tables owned by a different Snowflake account through a Horizon Catalog integration, without creating, storing or rotating any secret. Authentication uses workload identity federation, Horizon vends short-lived storage credentials, both accounts work on the same files with no copy, and it covers cross-region access, catalog-linked databases and private connectivity.
items.why: Sharing one copy of a table between business units or regions used to mean a service user, a key pair and a rotation runbook per link. Federated identity plus vended credentials removes the long-lived secret, which is the part security reviews and incidents care about, and keeps a single source of truth instead of two drifting copies.
items.try: In the 8.5 chapter's two-engine design, add a second Snowflake account that writes to the same Iceberg table. Write down who commits to the catalog, how a concurrent write from each account is resolved (optimistic commit on the metadata pointer), and what credential each side holds before and after this change.

items.title: BigQuery queries Iceberg tables in Unity Catalog, Glue and Snowflake Horizon in place, with an opt-in cross-cloud cache (GA)
items.summary: Released on 2 November 2026. BigQuery's Lakehouse federated catalogs now reach remote Iceberg catalogs as a GA feature: Databricks Unity Catalog, AWS Glue Data Catalog, Snowflake Horizon Catalog and Workday Data Lake, from BigQuery and Spark, without migrating data, over the internet or Cross-Cloud Interconnect and inside VPC Service Controls. A separate GA option caches the remote files in your Google Cloud region to cut egress and speed up repeat queries; it is off by default.
items.why: 'One table, many engines' now crosses clouds and vendors through the catalog, not through copies. The cost question moves to egress: every remote scan pays transfer unless you cache, and a cache brings a freshness question you must answer in the design.
items.try: Take a 2 TB table read daily from another cloud. Using the unit-costs table in module 10, price a full scan per day with and without the regional cache, then list what a stale cached file could break and how you would detect it.

items.title: BigQuery: change history (APPENDS) and continuous queries now work on Iceberg managed tables (GA)
items.summary: Released on 2 November 2026. The APPENDS table-valued function returns the rows appended to a BigQuery-managed Iceberg table over a time range, and BigQuery continuous queries can read new rows from these tables and write results back into them. On 3 November continuous queries also gained persistent and temporary SQL UDFs.
items.why: Incremental processing over an open table no longer needs a watermark column you maintain yourself: the engine tells you what was appended since a time. It is append-only, though, so updates and deletes still need CDC-style merge logic, which is exactly the distinction interviewers probe.
items.try: In the 6.3 lab, write the incremental step twice: once with a high-water-mark column and once as 'rows appended since the last run time'. Then add an update to an existing row and show which version misses it and why.

items.title: dbt's remote MCP server lands on Databricks Marketplace and checks permissions on every tool call
items.summary: In dbt's November 2026 release notes. The remote dbt MCP server can be installed from Databricks Marketplace. Each tool call is now checked against the project, environment, job or run it targets, calls without permission fail early with clearer errors, service tokens can use text_to_sql, and read-only users can query metrics through a shared analytics credential an admin sets up.
items.why: This is the 'tools, not passwords' pattern from A4.4 shipped by a vendor: the agent gets narrow tools, and authorization is decided per call on the object touched, not once per session. It is a ready answer to 'how do you stop an agent reading what the user can't'.
items.try: For the read-only data tool in Lab A4.3, write the per-call check: given a user, a tool and a target model, return allow or deny, and add three tests (allowed metric, model in another project, a write tool called by a read-only user).

items.title: dbt Core 1.13.0-rc1 drops Python 3.10, and dbt v2.0.11 renames --run-cache-mode to --state-mode
items.summary: dbt-core 1.13.0-rc1 was released on 4 November 2026 as a pre-release; it drops Python 3.10, which is end of life, and accepts the v2-only keys (info_schema, check-paths, checks) in dbt_project.yml. dbt v2.0.11 on 3 November renamed --run-cache-mode to --state-mode (the old flag stays as a deprecated alias) and DBT_AI_PROVIDER to DBT_ENGINE_AI_PROVIDER. In Studio IDE, v2 runs now follow the threads value in your credentials rather than the v2 default.
items.why: CI images pinned to Python 3.10 will fail on the next upgrade, and scripts using the old flag or environment variable will warn now and break later. Threads changing under you changes warehouse concurrency and cost without any code change.
items.try: In the 4.6 dbt project, list the Python version, flags and environment variables your CI job depends on, and write the one-line change each needs for 1.13 and v2.0.11. Then predict what happens to run time and warehouse load if threads drops from 48 to 4.

items.title: Airflow 3.4.0: task loops, a draining state, and breaking defaults for Python, Postgres and asset runs
items.summary: Released on 6 November 2026. Task groups can now repeat at runtime with .loop() (an until condition and a max_iterations cap), an experimental Dag importer accepts Dags written in TypeScript, Go, Java or YAML, and a new 'draining' Dag state lets active runs finish and then pauses the Dag. Breaking: Python 3.11 or later is required, the Dataset alias is gone from the airflow module (use Asset from airflow.sdk), psycopg3 (postgresql+psycopg://) is the Postgres driver, asset-triggered Dags start one run per event instead of batching events, and try_number on an up_for_retry task now points at the next try.
items.why: Upgrades break on exactly these lines: the metadata database connection string, old Dataset imports, and Dags that assumed several asset events would be batched into one run. Loops and draining are new tools for polling patterns and safe deploys that interviewers increasingly ask about.
items.try: In projects/lakehouse/airflow/dags/lakehouse_daily.py, list every import and connection string an upgrade to 3.4 would touch, then sketch how a downstream Dag triggered by the daily table asset would behave if three events arrived in one minute (three runs now, not one) and whether its tasks are idempotent enough for that.
